Inside the race to build quantum error correction

Published 2026-10-06 08:30 UTC

Quantum computers promise to solve certain problems far faster than ordinary computers, but they are plagued by errors. Their basic units, qubits, are fragile and lose their delicate quantum states through tiny disturbances. For years, the field's central challenge has been quantum error correction: spreading information across many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and fixed.

This year, several laboratories crossed what researchers call the break-even threshold. Their encoded logical qubits, built from dozens of physical qubits, preserved information longer than the best individual physical qubit in the same system. That milestone shows the error correction is removing more errors than it introduces.

The leading approach uses a scheme called the surface code, which arranges qubits in a grid. Some qubits store data while others repeatedly check their neighbors for errors without disturbing the stored information. A classical computer reads those checks and works out which corrections to apply, a process that must happen in microseconds.

Different groups are pursuing different hardware. Superconducting circuits operate at temperatures close to absolute zero and have fast operations. Trapped ions and neutral atoms have slower operations but longer-lived qubits and more flexible connections between them. Each platform has its own trade-offs for scaling up error correction.

Researchers emphasize that break-even is only a beginning. Useful quantum computers will need logical qubits with error rates millions of times lower than today's, which will require thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit with current designs. New codes that need fewer physical qubits are an active area of research.

Still, the results have changed the tone of the field. For the first time, experimentalists can show that adding more qubits to an error-correcting code makes the stored information more reliable, which is the behavior theory has long predicted.
